With the predictors rescaled, R-hat is 1.00, every bulk ESS is above 3,000, and there are no divergent transitions. Stan produces about 660 effective samples per second, compared with 0.3.
Part 3

# sd of each predictor on its original scale
hks |>
  select(troopLag, policeLag, militaryobserversLag, brv_AllLag,
         osvAllLagDum, incomp, epduration, lntpop) |>
  map_dbl(sd)

            troopLag            policeLag militaryobserversLag 
           2.8558605            0.1418510            0.1059394 
          brv_AllLag         osvAllLagDum               incomp 
         118.8278892            0.4253317            0.4648971 
          epduration               lntpop 
          52.5904099            1.2084279 



# original scales, but adapt_delta = 0.99
fit_mcmc_99 <- brm(
  f,
  data = hks,
  family = negbinomial,
  chains = 4,
  cores = 4,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),  # from default of 0.8
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  seed = 1234)


sps(fit_mcmc_99)[c("sps", "divergences", "max_rhat")]

$sps
[1] 0.1502428

$divergences
[1] 1877

$max_rhat
[1] 3.020168


On their original scales, the predictors’ SDs range from 0.1 (militaryobserversLag) to 119 (brv_AllLag), a factor of more than 1,000. So the plausible values of the coefficients differ in scale by about as much. Stan starts every coefficient at a random value between −2 and 2 and tunes its step sizes during warmup. With scales this different, those starting values are absurd for some coefficients (e.g., a coefficient of 2 on brv_AllLag, whose SD is 119, moves the log of the expected count by hundreds), and warmup doesn’t recover. After rescaling, every predictor has SD of about 0.5 (arm::rescale() only centers the two binary predictors), so the coefficients are on similar scales.
Raising adapt_delta doesn’t help here. With adapt_delta = 0.99, there are still 1,877 divergent transitions and R-hat is 3.02. A higher adapt_delta is the usual fix for divergent transitions, but here the problem is the scales. This is why we rescale by default.

title: Week 7 Exercises
text:
Exercise 6 Perot
Let’s return to the 1992 presidential vote (Bush, Clinton, and Perot), but now use Adolph’s specification rather than the notes’ model with party ID and the economy. In this exercise, you’ll use {marginaleffects} to compute and interpret the multinomial logit probabilities.
The data come from the same ANES file as the notes. We have 466 voters with complete data on these variables (Bush 184, Clinton 191, Perot 91). The variables are:

ideology: self-placement from 1 (very liberal) to 7 (very conservative)
ideology_distance: the distance between the respondent’s own ideology and where they place Bush on the same scale (0 to 6)
economy: the national economy compared with a year ago, from 1 (much better) to 5 (much worse)
gulf_war: 1 if the respondent thinks the Gulf War was worth it, 0 otherwise
nonwhite: 1 if the respondent is nonwhite, 0 otherwise


# load data; keep complete cases on the model's variables
perot_vote <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/data/bush-approval-1992.csv") |>
  select(vote_1992, ideology, ideology_distance, economy, gulf_war, nonwhite) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(vote_1992 = factor(vote_1992, levels = c("Bush", "Clinton", "Perot")))

# fit multinomial logit; the first level (Bush) is the baseline
perot_fit <- nnet::multinom(vote_1992 ~ ideology + ideology_distance + economy + gulf_war + nonwhite,
                            data = perot_vote, trace = FALSE)
coef(perot_fit)

        (Intercept)    ideology ideology_distance   economy   gulf_war
Clinton   -1.134040 -0.52504754         0.7920291 0.5969867 -0.7615256
Perot     -2.146247 -0.07646878         0.6818460 0.2918575 -0.3114140
          nonwhite
Clinton  0.7537022
Perot   -0.9945756



Compute the softmax of the linear predictors \((0, 1, -1)\). Then add 2 to each linear predictor and compute the softmax again. What do you notice?
Use predictions(..., type = "probs", newdata = datagrid(...)) to compute Pr(Bush), Pr(Clinton), and Pr(Perot) for a moderate (ideology 4) whose ideology is 2 points from where they place Bush, who thinks the economy is somewhat worse (economy 4), who thinks the Gulf War was worth it, and who is white.
Relevel the outcome so that Clinton is the baseline and refit the model. Which coefficients change? How do the new coefficients relate to the old ones? Are the probabilities from part 2 the same?
Plot the three probabilities as ideology moves from 1 to 7, holding the other variables at their part 2 values. Use comparisons() to compute the change in each probability from 1 to 7. Compare the direction of Pr(Perot) with the sign of Perot’s ideology coefficient. What do you notice?

Hint 1
For part 1, \(\Pr(Y = j) = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_k e^{z_k}}\). In R, that’s exp(z) / sum(exp(z)).

Hint 2
For part 3, use relevel(vote_1992, ref = "Clinton") or factor(..., levels = c("Clinton", "Bush", "Perot")). The refit’s estimates can differ from the ones you compute by hand in the fourth decimal (because of the optimizer’s tolerance).
For part 4, adapt the notes’ predictions() and geom_ribbon() code, with datagrid(ideology = 1:7, ...). Give the other four variables explicitly.

Complete solution
Part 1

# softmax of (0, 1, -1), then of (2, 3, 1)
perot_softmax <- function(z) exp(z) / sum(exp(z))
perot_softmax(c(0, 1, -1))

[1] 0.24472847 0.66524096 0.09003057

perot_softmax(c(0, 1, -1) + 2)

[1] 0.24472847 0.66524096 0.09003057


Both times, the probabilities are 0.245, 0.665, and 0.090. Adding the same constant to every linear predictor doesn’t change the probabilities. The \(e^{2}\) cancels.
\[
\Pr(Y = j) = \frac{e^{z_j + 2}}{\sum_k e^{z_k + 2}} = \frac{e^{2} e^{z_j}}{e^{2} \sum_k e^{z_k}} = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_k e^{z_k}}.
\]
This is why we can fix the baseline’s linear predictor at 0.
Part 2

# probabilities for the respondent
perot_profile <- datagrid(model = perot_fit, ideology = 4, ideology_distance = 2,
                          economy = 4, gulf_war = 1, nonwhite = 0)
predictions(perot_fit, newdata = perot_profile, type = "probs")


   Group ideology ideology_distance economy gulf_war nonwhite Estimate
 Bush           4                 2       4        1        0    0.361
 Clinton        4                 2       4        1        0    0.353
 Perot          4                 2       4        1        0    0.286
 Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
     0.0431 8.38   <0.001 54.0 0.277  0.446
     0.0398 8.86   <0.001 60.1 0.275  0.431
     0.0360 7.96   <0.001 49.0 0.216  0.357

Type: probs


The probabilities are 0.361 (Bush), 0.353 (Clinton), and 0.286 (Perot).
For this moderate, Bush and Clinton nearly tie, and Pr(Perot) is about 0.29.
Part 3

# Clinton as the baseline
perot_vote_clinton <- perot_vote |>
  mutate(vote_1992 = relevel(vote_1992, ref = "Clinton"))
perot_fit_clinton <- nnet::multinom(vote_1992 ~ ideology + ideology_distance + economy + gulf_war + nonwhite,
                                    data = perot_vote_clinton, trace = FALSE)
coef(perot_fit_clinton)

      (Intercept)  ideology ideology_distance    economy  gulf_war   nonwhite
Bush     1.133744 0.5250520        -0.7920126 -0.5969593 0.7616524 -0.7537098
Perot   -1.012627 0.4485993        -0.1101432 -0.3050862 0.4501643 -1.7484834

# the same thing from the Bush-baseline fit: differences of the old rows
rbind(Bush  = 0 - coef(perot_fit)["Clinton", ],
      Perot = coef(perot_fit)["Perot", ] - coef(perot_fit)["Clinton", ])

      (Intercept)  ideology ideology_distance    economy  gulf_war   nonwhite
Bush     1.134040 0.5250475        -0.7920291 -0.5969867 0.7615256 -0.7537022
Perot   -1.012207 0.4485788        -0.1101831 -0.3051292 0.4501116 -1.7482778


\[
\beta_{\text{Bush} \mid \text{Clinton}} = -\beta_{\text{Clinton} \mid \text{Bush}},
\qquad
\beta_{\text{Perot} \mid \text{Clinton}} = \beta_{\text{Perot} \mid \text{Bush}} - \beta_{\text{Clinton} \mid \text{Bush}}
\]

# probabilities for the part 2 respondent, both fits
perot_p_bush <- predictions(perot_fit, newdata = perot_profile, type = "probs")
perot_p_clinton <- predictions(perot_fit_clinton, newdata = perot_profile, type = "probs")
perot_p_bush |> select(group, estimate)


   Group Estimate
 Bush       0.361
 Clinton    0.353
 Perot      0.286

perot_p_clinton |> select(group, estimate)


   Group Estimate
 Clinton    0.353
 Bush       0.361
 Perot      0.286

# same log-likelihood
logLik(perot_fit)

'log Lik.' -353.5879 (df=12)

logLik(perot_fit_clinton)

'log Lik.' -353.5879 (df=12)


Every coefficient changes. The new Bush row is minus the old Clinton row (e.g., ideology 0.525, nonwhite −0.754). The new Perot row is the old Perot row minus the old Clinton row (e.g., ideology −0.076 − (−0.525) = 0.449; nonwhite −0.995 − 0.754 ≈ −1.75).
These differences match the refit to the third or fourth decimal (e.g., gulf_war 0.7617 vs. 0.7615). The gap comes from the optimizer’s tolerance.
The probabilities are identical to three decimals (0.361, 0.353, 0.286), and the log-likelihood is −353.59 for both fits. This is the same model with a different parameterization (i.e., the identification point from the notes).
Notice that relative to Clinton, Perot’s ideology coefficient is +0.45 (SE 0.10). We’ll need this in part 4.
Part 4

# probability of each candidate as ideology varies, other variables at the part 2 values
perot_p_ideology <- predictions(perot_fit,
                                newdata = datagrid(ideology = 1:7, ideology_distance = 2,
                                                   economy = 4, gulf_war = 1, nonwhite = 0),
                                type = "probs")

# plot
ggplot(perot_p_ideology, aes(x = ideology, y = estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high,
                             color = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(x = "Ideology (1 = very liberal, 7 = very conservative)", y = "Probability",
       color = "Candidate", fill = "Candidate")









# change in each candidate's probability from very liberal (1) to very conservative (7)
comparisons(perot_fit,
            variables = list(ideology = c(1, 7)),
            newdata = datagrid(ideology_distance = 2, economy = 4, gulf_war = 1, nonwhite = 0),
            type = "probs")


   Group ideology_distance economy gulf_war nonwhite Estimate Std. Error     z
 Bush                    2       4        1        0    0.397     0.1033  3.84
 Clinton                 2       4        1        0   -0.592     0.0875 -6.77
 Perot                   2       4        1        0    0.195     0.0930  2.10
 Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 % 97.5 %
   <0.001 13.0  0.1944  0.599
   <0.001 36.1 -0.7639 -0.421
   0.0356  4.8  0.0131  0.378

Term: ideology
Type: probs
Comparison: 7 - 1


Perot’s ideology coefficient is negative (−0.08, relative to Bush), but Pr(Perot) rises steadily, from 0.15 at 1 to 0.29 at 4 and 0.34 at 7. The change is 0.20 (95% CI from 0.01 to 0.38).
Why? Perot’s coefficient (−0.08) sits between Bush’s (0) and Clinton’s (−0.53). As ideology moves from 1 to 7, Pr(Clinton) falls by 0.59, and Perot gets part of that. Relative to Clinton, Perot’s coefficient is +0.45 (part 3).
The sign of Perot’s coefficient is itself uncertain (the SE of 0.11 is larger than the estimate of 0.08). Either way, the lesson is the same. Compute the probabilities.
gulf_war shows the same thing. Perot’s coefficient is −0.31, but Pr(Perot) rises from 0.26 to 0.29 (the CI includes 0). And economy gives a non-monotone Pr(Perot), which peaks at 4 (0.29) and dips at 5 (0.28), even though the coefficient is positive (0.29).
One caveat: holding distance at 2 while ideology moves from 1 to 7 extrapolates. No respondent with ideology 1 has distance 2, and only 3 respondents with ideology 7 do.

title: Week 7 Exercises
section: Exercise 7 Red State, Blue State: Part 3
text:
Exercise 7 Red State, Blue State: Part 3
In Parts 2(a) and 2(b), we modeled party ID. Now let’s model the vote itself in the 2024 election, in the same two states. Recall Figure 4 in Gelman et al. (2007, p. 356). In 2000–2004, richer Mississippians voted Republican, but income barely mattered in Connecticut.
The data come from the 2024 CES. vote is “Did not vote” (i.e., no validated record of voting), “Harris”, or “Trump” (i.e., the vote reported in the post-election survey). income is the same five-point scale as in Part 2 (from −2 to 2).
Income might matter for whether people vote, not only for whom they vote. We have three outcomes with no order (did not vote, Harris, and Trump), so we need a multinomial logit.

# load data; Mississippi and Connecticut
ms_vote <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/red-state-part3-mississippi.csv")
ct_vote <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/red-state-part3-connecticut.csv")


Fit brm(vote ~ income, family = categorical()) in each state, with Harris as the baseline. What does each set of coefficients compare?
Use predictions() to compute the probability of each outcome at each income category. Make a stacked plot with one panel per state. What changes with income? Turnout? Vote choice? Both?
Use comparisons() to compute the change in the probability of each outcome as income moves from −1 to 1, in each state, with 90% CIs. Does income still matter more for the Trump vote in Mississippi?
Fit the Mississippi model without income (vote ~ 1) and with income as a factor (vote ~ income_factor, where income_factor = factor(income)). Compare these two models with the income model using loo() and loo_compare(). Does income improve the prediction? Does treating income as a factor improve it further?

Hint 1
For part 1, factor(vote, levels = c("Harris", "Trump", "Did not vote")) makes Harris the baseline (i.e., the first level).

Hint 2
For parts 2 and 3, predictions() and comparisons() work on a brm() fit just as on a multinom() fit, except that you leave out type = "probs". The group column holds the outcome. The intervals are posterior intervals.

Hint 3
For part 4, see “Interpreting elpd_diff and se_diff” in the LOOIC chapter. If loo() flags observations with a high Pareto \(\hat{k}\), see the chapter’s “Fixing high \(\hat{k}\)” section.

Complete solution
Part 1

# harris as the baseline
ms_vote <- ms_vote |>
  mutate(vote = factor(vote, levels = c("Harris", "Trump", "Did not vote")))
ct_vote <- ct_vote |>
  mutate(vote = factor(vote, levels = c("Harris", "Trump", "Did not vote")))

# multinomial logit in each state
fit_ms_vote <- brm(vote ~ income, data = ms_vote,
                   family = categorical(link = "logit"),
                   backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234)
fit_ct_vote <- brm(vote ~ income, data = ct_vote,
                   family = categorical(link = "logit"),
                   backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234)


fixef(fit_ms_vote)

                         Estimate Est.Error        Q2.5      Q97.5
muTrump_Intercept       0.3288210 0.1485683  0.03176500  0.6317121
muDidnotvote_Intercept  0.9136666 0.1405976  0.63879890  1.1903143
muTrump_income          0.2043992 0.1518013 -0.09262864  0.5080977
muDidnotvote_income    -0.5673395 0.1322043 -0.82865767 -0.3036846

fixef(fit_ct_vote)

                          Estimate  Est.Error       Q2.5      Q97.5
muTrump_Intercept      -0.72719080 0.13819687 -0.9964379 -0.4573522
muDidnotvote_Intercept  0.31134849 0.10340930  0.1149826  0.5170650
muTrump_income         -0.00188958 0.12692385 -0.2512843  0.2474895
muDidnotvote_income    -0.46287657 0.09461065 -0.6445496 -0.2746005


Each set of coefficients gives the log odds of that outcome vs. Harris (e.g., muTrump_income compares Trump with Harris). For “Did not vote”, the income coefficient is −0.57 in Mississippi and −0.46 in Connecticut. Richer people are less likely to stay home (relative to voting for Harris). For Trump, the income coefficient is 0.20 in Mississippi and 0.00 in Connecticut.
Part 2

p_vote <- bind_rows(
  Mississippi = predictions(fit_ms_vote, newdata = datagrid(income = -2:2)),
  Connecticut = predictions(fit_ct_vote, newdata = datagrid(income = -2:2)),
  .id = "state"
)

ggplot(p_vote, aes(x = income, y = estimate, fill = group)) +
  geom_area(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(state)) +
  labs(x = "Income category", y = "Probability", fill = NULL)








Pr(did not vote) falls from 0.80 to 0.20 in Mississippi and from 0.70 to 0.27 in Connecticut.
In Mississippi, Pr(Trump) rises from 0.10 to 0.53, and Pr(Harris) rises too, from 0.10 to 0.26. In Connecticut, Pr(Harris) rises from 0.20 to 0.49 and Pr(Trump) from 0.10 to 0.24.
So income changes both, but mostly turnout. Notice that richer Mississippians are more likely to vote for Harris than poorer Mississippians are, because poorer Mississippians mostly don’t vote.
Part 3

comparisons(fit_ms_vote, variables = list(income = c(-1, 1)), newdata = datagrid(grid_type = "mean_or_mode"), conf_level = 0.9)


        Group Estimate   5.0 % 95.0 %
 Harris         0.0888  0.0224  0.157
 Trump          0.2382  0.1584  0.319
 Did not vote  -0.3293 -0.4026 -0.251

Term: income
Type: response
Comparison: 1 - -1

comparisons(fit_ct_vote, variables = list(income = c(-1, 1)), newdata = datagrid(grid_type = "mean_or_mode"), conf_level = 0.9)


        Group Estimate   5.0 % 95.0 %
 Harris         0.1527  0.0897  0.217
 Trump          0.0728  0.0217  0.123
 Did not vote  -0.2261 -0.2901 -0.158

Term: income
Type: response
Comparison: 1 - -1


In Mississippi, Pr(did not vote) changes by −0.33 (90% interval from −0.40 to −0.25), Pr(Harris) by 0.09 (0.02 to 0.16), and Pr(Trump) by 0.24 (0.16 to 0.32).
In Connecticut, Pr(did not vote) changes by −0.23 (−0.29 to −0.16), Pr(Harris) by 0.15 (0.09 to 0.22), and Pr(Trump) by 0.07 (0.02 to 0.12).
Income matters much more for turnout than for vote choice. But income still matters more for the Trump vote in Mississippi (0.24 vs. 0.07). Notice that these are changes in Pr(Trump) among all respondents, not only among voters.
Part 4

# mississippi model without income
fit_ms_null <- brm(vote ~ 1, data = ms_vote,
                   family = categorical(link = "logit"),
                   backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234)


# mississippi model with income as a factor (a separate effect for each category);
# create the factor as a column (factor() inside the formula breaks reloo)
ms_vote <- ms_vote |>
  mutate(income_factor = factor(income))
fit_ms_factor <- brm(vote ~ income_factor, data = ms_vote,
                     family = categorical(link = "logit"),
                     backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234)


loo_ms_null <- loo(fit_ms_null)
loo_ms_vote <- loo(fit_ms_vote)
loo_ms_factor <- loo(fit_ms_factor)

Warning: Found 2 observations with a pareto_k > 0.7 in model 'fit_ms_factor'.
We recommend to set 'moment_match = TRUE' in order to perform moment matching
for problematic observations.

loo_compare(loo_ms_null, loo_ms_vote, loo_ms_factor)

         model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff      diag_elpd
   fit_ms_vote       0.0     0.0      NA                         
 fit_ms_factor      -8.8     2.7    1.00           2 k_psis > 0.7
   fit_ms_null     -23.2     6.9    1.00                         



Diagnostic flags present.
See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`)
or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html.


The model with income (one slope for each outcome) is best. The intercept-only model is worse by 23.2 elpd, with se_diff 6.9 (i.e., a LOOIC difference of 46.4). That’s well over 4 and about 3.4 SEs, so by the rules of thumb it’s a meaningful difference. Income improves the prediction, mostly through turnout (part 3).
The factor model is worse than the income model by 8.8 elpd (se_diff 2.7). But diag_elpd flags 2 observations with Pareto \(\hat{k} > 0.7\), so its PSIS estimate isn’t reliable. Both are in the top income category, which has only 4 Mississippians, so the factor model’s estimates for that category lean heavily on each of them. Let’s refit for those two observations.

# exact loo for the flagged observations in the factor model
reloo_ms_factor <- loo(fit_ms_factor, reloo = TRUE, reloo_args = list(seed = 1234))


loo_compare(loo_ms_null, loo_ms_vote, reloo_ms_factor)

         model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff diag_elpd
   fit_ms_vote       0.0     0.0      NA                    
 fit_ms_factor     -16.7     8.2    0.98                    
   fit_ms_null     -23.2     6.9    1.00                    


With exact LOO for those two observations, the factor model is worse by 16.7 elpd (se_diff 8.2, about 2 SEs). PSIS was too optimistic about the factor model.
So treating income as a factor doesn’t improve the prediction. It makes it worse. The factor model has 10 coefficients (an intercept and four income effects for each of the two non-baseline outcomes), compared with 4 for the income model, and the extra ones are estimated from very few respondents.

title: Week 7 Exercises
section: Exercise 8 Polynomials in age and the LOOIC
text:
Exercise 8 Polynomials in age and the LOOIC
In the LOOIC chapter, we compared models with linear and cubic age for the turnout data. Now let’s consider every polynomial in age from degree 1 (linear) to degree 9.
The code below fits the nine models with brm(), computes LOO for each, plots the LOOIC against the degree, and compares the models with loo_compare(). You don’t need to run it. Use the output to answer the questions below.

# load only the turnout data frame and create rescaled columns
turnout <- ZeligData::turnout |>
  mutate(across(age:income, arm::rescale, .names = "rs_{.col}"))


# fit the model with a polynomial in age of each degree from 1 to 9
# (poly() uses orthogonal polynomials, so the high powers don't blow up)
fits_poly <- map(1:9, \(degree) {
  f <- as.formula(paste0("vote ~ poly(age, ", degree, ") + rs_educate + rs_income + race"))
  brm(f, data = turnout, family = bernoulli,
      backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1234)
})
names(fits_poly) <- paste("degree", 1:9)

# loo for each model; reloo = TRUE refits the model without each observation
# that has a high Pareto k (> 0.7) and computes exact LOO for it (see the notes)
loos_poly <- map(fits_poly, \(fit) loo(fit, reloo = TRUE, reloo_args = list(seed = 1234)))


# looic, its se, and p_loo for each model
looic_poly <- tibble(
  degree = 1:9,
  looic = map_dbl(loos_poly, \(l) l$estimates["looic", "Estimate"]),
  se = map_dbl(loos_poly, \(l) l$estimates["looic", "SE"]),
  p_loo = map_dbl(loos_poly, \(l) l$estimates["p_loo", "Estimate"])
)
looic_poly

# A tibble: 9 × 4
  degree looic    se p_loo
   <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1      1 2034.  46.0  5.10
2      2 2022.  46.5  6.20
3      3 2023.  46.6  7.34
4      4 2025.  46.6  8.42
5      5 2026.  46.7  9.29
6      6 2024.  46.8 10.0 
7      7 2021.  47.0 11.3 
8      8 2023.  47.2 12.9 
9      9 2024.  47.2 13.5 

ggplot(looic_poly, aes(x = degree, y = looic)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  labs(x = "Degree of the polynomial in age", y = "LOOIC")









# compare the nine models
loo_compare(loos_poly)

    model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse       diag_diff diag_elpd
 degree 7       0.0     0.0      NA                          
 degree 2      -0.2     3.3    0.52 |elpd_diff| < 4          
 degree 3      -0.7     3.2    0.59 |elpd_diff| < 4          
 degree 8      -0.8     1.5    0.70 |elpd_diff| < 4          
 degree 6      -1.2     2.3    0.70 |elpd_diff| < 4          
 degree 9      -1.3     1.7    0.78 |elpd_diff| < 4          
 degree 4      -1.8     3.2    0.72 |elpd_diff| < 4          
 degree 5      -2.4     3.1    0.78 |elpd_diff| < 4          
 degree 1      -6.2     5.1    0.89                          



Which model has the lowest LOOIC?
Compare the best and second-best models using elpd_diff and se_diff. How strong is the evidence for the best model over the second best?
Compare the best model with the linear model (degree 1) the same way. How strong is the evidence now?
If you had to choose one model, which would you choose? Why?

Hint
See “Interpreting elpd_diff and se_diff” in the LOOIC chapter. Remember that the LOOIC difference is −2 × elpd_diff.

Complete solution
Part 1
Degree 7 has the lowest LOOIC (2021.4), so it’s at the top of the table.
The LOOIC drops from 2034 (linear) to 2022 (quadratic). For degrees 2 through 9, it moves between 2021 and 2026, with no clear trend.
Each LOOIC has an SE of about 46, which is much larger than the differences. But I left those SEs off the plot. We compare the models on the same respondents, so the SE that matters is se_diff (i.e., the SE of the difference).
p_loo grows from 5.1 (degree 1) to 13.5 (degree 9), about one per added term. This is close to \(k\) = degree + 4, as we expect for a model that fits well.
Part 2
The second-best model is degree 2, with elpd_diff = −0.2 and se_diff = 3.3. Because |elpd_diff| < 4, the two models predict about equally well.
So we have no evidence for the best model over the second best. In fact, every model from degree 2 to 9 is within 2.4 elpd of the best.
Part 3
For the linear model, elpd_diff = −6.2 and se_diff = 5.1 (i.e., a LOOIC difference of 12.4).
This difference is larger than 4, but it’s only about 1.2 SEs. This is modest evidence that age needs a curve. It’s close to the chapter’s comparison of the linear and cubic models (5.8, with se_diff 4.1).
Part 4
By the rules of thumb, no difference here is clearly meaningful. Degrees 2 through 9 are all within 4 elpd of the best, and the linear model is more than 4 behind but only about 1.2 SEs.
If I had to choose, I’d choose the quadratic. It predicts about as well as the best model, it’s the simplest model with a curve in age, and the curve has some (modest) support over the line. Other choices are reasonable if you defend them with elpd_diff and se_diff (e.g., the linear model for simplicity, given the modest evidence against it).

Exercise 1 Provide Feedback
Your peer review is due before class on Tuesday, October 27. I sent the pairs and instructions by email.
Provide comments on your assigned paper. When providing feedback on colleagues’ work, I like the RAP model here. Most importantly, in this model, “focus time and effort on the highest points of leverage for improving the document.”

In addition to other comments, please make sure to provide feedback on these three items:

Does the paper make a clear descriptive claim? It might be helpful to review the key readings on descriptive research here, such as Gerring (2012), Holmes et al. (2024), and de Kadt and Grzymala-Busse (2025).
Does the paper make a compelling empirical argument for that descriptive claim?
Does the paper clearly explain the substantive/theoretical/normative importance of that descriptive claim? It’s important that the defense not rely on any assumed/implied causal relationship among the variables.

title: Week 9 Exercises
text:
Exercise 8 Simulate and Recover; Logit
One important way to test and develop your understanding of statistical models and quantities of interest is to simulate a fake data set with known true quantity of interest (e.g., coefficients or first difference) and then recover that quantity of interest through your estimation procedure.
Do this for logistic regression. As your quantity of interest, use the first difference as one variable moves from the minimum to the maximum with other variables at their mean or mode.

First, simulate a fake data set with a known quantity of interest. Have your agent write this part with the prompt below.1
Second, we can use glm() and {marginaleffects} to recover the true quantity of interest—it should usually be in the 95% CI.
Third, adapt this code to compute the truth for the quantity of interest computed by avg_comparisons(fit, variables = list(x1 = "minmax")).
For this particular version of the simulation and recover exercise, the quantities of interest in (2) and (3) seem similar, but they give different answers–the estimate for (3) is much larger than the estimate for (2). Why?

Start the agent in an empty folder and give it this prompt.
Write an R script named simulate-logit.R that simulates a fake data set from a logit model. I'll use it later to check whether glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial) recovers the true values. Follow these rules.

- Put set.seed() at the top. Then set the sample size n once. Make it at least 10,000.
- Create one numeric explanatory variable x1, drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and SD 0.5.
- Create one qualitative explanatory variable x2 with two labels. Make one label much more common than the other (about 75% vs. 25%).
- Choose the true coefficients (an intercept, a coefficient for x1, and a coefficient for x2, each between -3 and 3) and put them together near the top of the script. Don't include an interaction. Choose values so that y = 1 is rare (a probability near 0.05) for the more common label of x2 and much more common (a probability near 0.5) for the less common label.
- Compute each observation's probability with plogis(). Then draw y (0 or 1) with rbinom().
- Put y, x1, and x2 together in one data frame named data.
- At the end, compute the true first difference: the change in the probability that y = 1 as x1 moves from its minimum to its maximum, with x2 at its most common label. Compute it from the true coefficients with plogis(), not from a fitted model.
- Comment each step using "comments showing intent." Write code that is readable for humans, not necessarily the most compact or efficient.
Hint
Your agent chooses the labels for x2. In datagrid(), use the more common one (e.g., datagrid(x2 = "common")).

Complete solution
Solution: (1)
Your script will differ. Here is one version.

# --- simulate a fake data set ---

# set sample size
n <- 100000  # needs to be large enough so that CI isn't super wide
# note: feel free to make the sample size VERY large in this exercise

# create explanatory variables
## numeric variable
x1 <- rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)  # sd = 0.5 is my preferred scale for interpretation
## qualitative variable
x2 <- sample(c("Label 1", "Label 2"),
             size = n,
             replace = TRUE,
             prob = c(0.75, 0.25))  # about 75% will be "Label 1"

# create coefficients
b0 <- 0
b1 <- 1
b2 <- -3

# simulate outcome for logit model
linpred <- b0 + b1*x1 + b2*(x2 == "Label 1")
p <- plogis(linpred)
y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = p)

# combine into data frame
data <- data.frame(y, x1, x2)

# truth: fd as x1 moves from min to max; x2 at mode
pr_hi <- plogis(b0 + b1*max(x1) + b2)
pr_lo <- plogis(b0 + b1*min(x1) + b2)
pr_hi - pr_lo

[1] 0.3032397


Solution: (2)

# load packages
library(marginaleffects)

# recover the first quantity of interest
fit <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = data, family = binomial)
comparisons(fit,
            variables = list(x1 = "minmax"),
            newdata = datagrid(x2 = "Label 1"))


      x2 Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
 Label 1     0.31     0.0101 30.8   <0.001 690.7  0.29   0.33

Term: x1
Type: response
Comparison: Max - Min


Solution: (3)

# truth: avg fd as x1 moves from min to max; x2 at all observed values
pr_hi <- plogis(b0 + b1*max(x1) + b2*(x2 == "Label 1"))
pr_lo <- plogis(b0 + b1*min(x1) + b2*(x2 == "Label 1"))
mean(pr_hi - pr_lo)

[1] 0.4250334

# recover this second quantity of interest
avg_comparisons(fit, variables = list(x1 = "minmax"))


 Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %
    0.433     0.0095 45.6   <0.001 Inf 0.414  0.452

Term: x1
Type: response
Comparison: Max - Min


Solution: (4)
The quantity of interest in (2) fixes x2 to "Label 1". The coefficients b0, b1, and b2 make it so that events are relatively rare when x2 equals "Label 1"—see the estimated probabilities (i.e., “expected values”) below. Because the probabilities are close to zero when x2 equals "Label 1", x1 has a smaller effect than when x2 equals "Label 2". I chose the variables and the coefficients to make this the case.

p <- predictions(fit)
ggplot(p, aes(x = x1, y = estimate, shape = x2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1)








The quantity of interest in (3) averages across the effects of x1 for the observed values of x2. This means that about 25% of the times, you’re getting the big Label 2 effect. And about 75% of the time, you’re getting the small Label 1 effect. Averaging these less common big effects and more common small effects gives a larger quantity than looking only at the more common small effect.

title: Week 9 Exercises
text:
Exercise 9 Replicate Jefferson (2024)
Jefferson (2024) [pdf] [supplement] argues that many Black Americans who call themselves “conservative” don’t use the label the way the liberal-conservative scale assumes. The replication code is on the Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/WDS0EP).
Use your agent to download the replication materials and reproduce every number in the article’s tables and figures (Tables 1–3 and Figures 1–4, plus the numbers in the text that come from them). Have the agent write a Quarto report that runs the code, shows each result next to the number printed in the paper, and tests each one with {testthat}. For example,
test_that("Table 1: correlation for Black respondents", {
  expect_equal(round(r_black, 2), 0.12)
})
The deposit has code but no data. The ANES Time Series Cumulative Data File requires a free account at electionstudies.org, so download it yourself and put it in the folder where you start the agent.

Which results reproduce? Which don’t? Why not?
What did the agent change to make the code run? Did it tell you about every change?
Check three tests by hand. Do they test what they claim to test? Did any test pass when it shouldn’t have?
What did you have to do yourself? What would you put in the prompt next time?

Hint 1
Give the agent the article and the supplement, the Dataverse DOI, and the path to the ANES file you downloaded. Tell it which surveys and years the paper uses. Ask it to work on copies of the authors’ scripts and to list every change it makes.

Hint 2
Ask for tests at the paper’s precision (e.g., round to two decimals before comparing with a number printed to two decimals). Ask the agent to report only what it ran, and to list the numbers it couldn’t test and why.

Hint 3
You don’t need the supplement’s telephone and web robustness section, the Cronbach’s alphas, or the 2012 percentages in footnote 4 (the deposit has no code for them). You don’t need to match the figures’ styling, rewrite the author’s code, or install an old version of R.

Complete solution
Your report will differ from ours. Here’s what a careful replication finds, checked against the ANES file that’s available now (the February 5, 2026 release).
Getting the code to run
The deposit is code only (three R scripts and a README). The scripts read the ANES cumulative file and the 2004–2016 ANES studies from the GitHub package jamesmartherus/anesr. Three problems stop the code as deposited.

rnr_create_tables_and_graphs.R doesn’t parse. Line 416 ends with + followed by two stray backticks.
stargazer 5.2.3 fails on R 4.2 and later (“the condition has length > 1”) when a stargazer() call spans several lines. (You can patch stargazer or check the numbers from the model objects instead.)
The scripts call View(), which stops a non-interactive run, and they expect jen_data/ and jen_output/ folders.

Getting the paper’s numbers
The README names an older release of the cumulative file (2021-11-18). The current release differs in three ways that matter here.

It adds 2024, which has 696 face-to-face interviews. The cleaning script keeps every face-to-face interview from 1972 on, with no end year. So Table 1 comes out as 0.45 (24,473 respondents) and 0.12 (4,296), against 0.44 (24,030) and 0.12 (4,210) in the paper. The table’s title still says “1972-2016.” Adding year <= 2016 to the filter fixes it.
For 2016, the liberal-conservative scale (VCF0803) is now the pre-election question (V161126). The older release used the post-election question (V162171), and the codebook still says it does. This changes 536 of the 1,180 face-to-face respondents in 2016 and moves Model 3 of Table 2 the most (e.g., the coefficient for ideology falls from 0.246 to 0.152). Replacing VCF0803 for 2016 with V162171 from the 2016 study fixes it (1–7 as is, 99 → 9, everything else → 0).
The 1976 weights are rescaled to average 1 (0.783 and 1.175 rather than 1 and 1.5). Dividing them by the smaller weight fixes it.

With these three changes, the cleaned data are identical to those built from the older release, and every number the code computes matches the paper. A few things in the paper have no code (the Cronbach’s alphas, the 2012 percentages in footnote 4, and the supplement’s telephone and web section). Tables 2 and 3 print p-values, but the code prints SEs, so I checked the p-values with t = coefficient / SE.
Tests
A test should compare the computed number with the number typed from the paper, at the paper’s precision.
test_that("Table 1 matches the paper", {
  expect_equal(round(r_white, 2), 0.44)
  expect_equal(n_white, 24030)
  expect_equal(round(r_black, 2), 0.12)
  expect_equal(n_black, 4210)
})
Check that the agent didn’t take the “expected” value from the output it’s testing, or loosen a tolerance until a test passed. Either makes a test that can’t fail. A test that runs on the current file without the year filter fails on the N’s, which is what we want it to do.

title: Week 9 Exercises
section: Exercise 10 Red State, Blue State: Part 4
text:
Exercise 10 Red State, Blue State: Part 4
In Parts 2(a), 2(b), and 3, we modeled party ID and the vote in Mississippi and Connecticut. Now let’s fit the same model in every state. Andrew Gelman calls this “the secret weapon”. We fit the same model to many data sets and then plot all the estimates together. (This sets up the hierarchical models, which use all the states at once.)
The data are the 48,582 CES 2024 respondents in the 50 states (no DC) who chose Harris or Trump before the election. vote_rep is 1 for Trump and 0 for Harris. For respondents who had already voted early, it’s their vote. For everyone else, it’s the candidate they preferred. income is the same five-point scale as in Parts 2 and 3 (from −2 to 2). state_median_income is the state’s median household income in thousands of dollars.

# load data; 50 states
ces <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/red-state-part4.csv")

In each state, fit the logit vote_rep ~ income. As the effect of income, use the change in Pr(Trump) as income moves from −1 to 1, with a 90% CI.
The “many models” workflow. The tidyverse has a workflow for fitting the same model to many groups (see the “Many models” chapter of the first edition of R for Data Science). It has three steps.

nest() collapses the data to one row per group. The group’s rows go into a list-column called data, so each element of data is a whole data frame.
map() applies a function to each element of a list-column. Inside mutate(), map(data, f) applies f() to each group’s data frame and stores the results in a new list-column (e.g., one fitted model per group).
unnest() expands a list-column of data frames back into ordinary rows and columns.

Here is a toy example. (\(d) is R’s shorthand for function(d).)

# toy example: one row per group, a summary for each group, then back to columns
toy <- tibble(group = c("a", "a", "b", "b"),
              y     = c(1, 3, 10, 14))
toy |>
  nest(data = -group) |>
  mutate(summary = map(data, \(d) tibble(mean_y = mean(d$y), sd_y = sd(d$y)))) |>
  unnest(summary)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  group data             mean_y  sd_y
  <chr> <list>            <dbl> <dbl>
1 a     <tibble [2 × 1]>      2  1.41
2 b     <tibble [2 × 1]>     12  2.83



Use the “many models” workflow to fit the logit in each state and compute the effect of income in each state.
Plot the 50 effects with their 90% CIs, sorted from largest to smallest, with the states on the vertical axis. Which states have the largest effects? Which have the smallest? Where are Mississippi and Connecticut? Which states have the widest CIs? Why?
Plot the effects against state_median_income, labeled with the state abbreviations. Does income matter more in poorer states? Which states don’t fit the pattern?

Hint 1
Ask your agent to adapt the toy example to these data. Then check one state by hand (i.e., fit its glm() and run comparisons() yourself).

Hint 2
comparisons(fit, variables = list(income = c(-1, 1)), newdata = datagrid(), conf_level = 0.9) returns one row (i.e., the effect of income for a typical respondent). (Income is the only variable in the model, so every respondent has the same effect.) For the sorted plot, reorder(state_abbr, estimate) orders the states by their effects.

Complete solution
Part 1
I wrote two small functions. One fits the logit to one state’s data. The other computes the effect of income from one fit.

# fit the logit to one state's data
fit_logit <- function(data) {
  glm(vote_rep ~ income, family = binomial, data = data)
}

# change in pr(trump) as income moves from -1 to 1, with a 90% ci
income_effect <- function(fit) {
  comparisons(fit,
              variables = list(income = c(-1, 1)),
              newdata = datagrid(),
              conf_level = 0.9) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
}

# many models: one row per state, one fit per state, one effect per state
ces_effects <- ces |>
  nest(data = -c(state_name, state_abbr, state_median_income)) |>
  mutate(n      = map_int(data, nrow),
         fit    = map(data, fit_logit),
         effect = map(fit, income_effect)) |>
  unnest(effect) |>
  select(state_abbr, state_median_income, n, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

ces_effects

Part 2

ggplot(ces_effects, aes(x = estimate, xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high,
                        y = reorder(state_abbr, estimate))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "Change in Pr(Trump) as income moves from −1 to 1 (90% CI)",
       y = NULL)

ces_effects |> arrange(desc(estimate)) |> head(3)

  mutate(width = conf.high - conf.low) |>
  arrange(desc(width)) |>
  head(5)

  state_abbr state_median_income     n estimate conf.low conf.high width
  <chr>                    <dbl> <int>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>

Mississippi has the largest effect. As income moves from −1 to 1, Pr(Trump) rises by about 0.15 (90% CI from 0.07 to 0.22). New Mexico and Louisiana are next (about 0.08 each). Oregon has the smallest effect (about −0.08, from −0.13 to −0.03), followed by Hawaii and Wyoming. Connecticut’s effect is about zero (from −0.06 to 0.07).
The widest CIs belong to the states with the fewest respondents: Wyoming (79 respondents), North Dakota, Alaska, Vermont, and South Dakota (all under about 150). The CI for Wyoming is about 0.33 wide, three times the median width (about 0.11). Two of the extreme effects (Hawaii and Wyoming) come from these small states. Their CIs easily include zero.
Part 3

# effects against state income
ggplot(ces_effects, aes(x = state_median_income, y = estimate,
                        ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_smooth(aes(ymin = NULL, ymax = NULL), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_errorbar(width = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_text(aes(label = state_abbr), size = 3) +
  labs(x = "State median household income ($1,000s)",
       y = "Change in Pr(Trump) as income\nmoves from −1 to 1 (90% CI)")







# correlation between state income and the effect
cor(ces_effects$state_median_income, ces_effects$estimate)

[1] -0.3294925


Yes, on average. The line slopes down, and the correlation between state income and the effect is about −0.33. Income matters most in poor Southern states (Mississippi and Louisiana) and least in rich states like Connecticut. But several states sit far from the line. Kentucky and Montana are poorer than the median state but have negative effects. Oregon, near the middle in income, has the most negative effect.

title: Week 9 Exercises
section: Exercise 11 Red State, Blue State: Part 5
text:
Exercise 11 Red State, Blue State: Part 5
The ANES, the survey political scientists most often use to study voters, is much smaller than the CES. In 2024, it has 2,445 respondents in the 50 states who chose Harris or Trump before the election (the CES has 48,582). vote_rep is measured as in Part 4.

# load data; 50 states
anes <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/red-state-part5.csv")


Repeat Exercise 10 with the ANES data.
What are the consequences of the smaller sample? How do the CIs compare with the CES? Which states can’t you estimate at all? Why not? Which states have the largest and smallest effects? Should we believe those effects? Does the pattern from Part 4 (larger effects in poorer states) still show up?

Hint 1
A logit needs both Trump and Harris supporters. It also fails when income separates them (e.g., every Trump supporter is richer than every Harris supporter). Count the respondents and the Trump supporters in each state. Look for CIs of width 0 or CIs that run past −1 or 1.

Hint 2
In a state where the logit can’t be estimated, comparisons() may return an error instead of a row. possibly(income_effect, otherwise = NULL) returns NULL instead of stopping, and unnest(effect, keep_empty = TRUE) keeps that state as a row of NAs.

Complete solution
Part 1

# many models on the anes; possibly() keeps going when a state can't be estimated
anes_effects <- anes |>
  nest(data = -c(state_name, state_abbr, state_median_income)) |>
  mutate(n       = map_int(data, nrow),
         n_trump = map_dbl(data, \(d) sum(d$vote_rep)),
         fit     = map(data, fit_logit),
         effect  = map(fit, possibly(income_effect, otherwise = NULL))) |>
  unnest(effect, keep_empty = TRUE) |>
  select(state_abbr, state_median_income, n, n_trump, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

# the smallest states
anes_effects |>
  arrange(n) |>
  print(n = 12)

The ANES has about 50 respondents per state; the CES has about 1,000.

The CIs are about four times wider. The median width is about 0.43 in the ANES and about 0.11 in the CES. Even California, the largest state in the ANES (206 respondents), has a CI about 0.18 wide. Some CIs run past −1 or 1 (e.g., South Dakota and New Hampshire), which is impossible for a change in a probability. These CIs are the estimate ± 1.64 SEs. That approximation fails with so few respondents.
Some states can’t be estimated at all. Wyoming has one respondent and Vermont has two, so comparisons() returns nothing. In other tiny states, the model breaks. Delaware (4 respondents) gives an effect of about 0 with a CI of width 0, and Alaska (4 respondents) gives a CI from about −6 to 6. Neither CI tells us anything about the effect.
The extreme effects are far more extreme than in the CES. The largest come from tiny states. South Dakota (7 respondents) and New Hampshire (5) are about 0.67, and Nevada (13) is about 0.50. At the other end, Oklahoma (18 respondents) is about −0.46 and Massachusetts (49) is about −0.38. In the CES, no state is above 0.15 or below −0.08. With so few respondents, the most extreme estimates are mostly noise.
Mississippi and Connecticut are hard to pin down. Connecticut’s effect is about 0.04 (from −0.17 to 0.25), close to the CES, but the CI is about three times as wide. Mississippi has 17 respondents. Its effect is about 0.11, with a CI from −0.19 to 0.41, which includes both zero and the CES estimate (0.15).
The pattern from Part 4 is still there among the larger states. Among the 30 states with at least 30 respondents, the correlation between state income and the effect is about −0.38, close to the CES (−0.33). But the small states’ estimates are so noisy that the plot against state income doesn’t show it.

Fitting each state separately works when each state has many respondents, as in the CES. In the ANES, most states have too few respondents to say much on their own. A hierarchical model lets those states borrow information from the other states.

title: Week 10 Exercises
section: Exercise 1 Simulate and Recover; Ordered Logit
text:
Exercise 1 Simulate and Recover; Ordered Logit
One important way to test and develop your understandings of statistical models and quantities of interest is to simulate a fake data set with known true quantity of interest (e.g., coefficients or first difference) and then recover that quantity of interest through your estimation procedure.

Week 9 did this for logit: Simulate and Recover; Logit.

Do this for the ordered logit model in the notes. As your quantity of interest, use \(\Pr(y \geq 3)\) when income equals 1.5 and x2 equals "Label 1".

First, simulate a fake data set with known cutpoints, coefficients, and quantity of interest. The code below handles this. Notice that the linear predictor eta has no intercept. The cutpoints alpha take its place.
Second, use MASS::polr() to fit an ordered logit model to the fake data. Are the true cutpoints and coefficients inside their 95% confidence intervals? (polr() calls the cutpoints “Intercepts” and labels them 1|2, 2|3, and 3|4.)
Third, use predictions() to recover the true quantity of interest. Is the true value inside the 95% CI?
Fourth, adapt the code to compute the true first difference in \(\Pr(y \geq 3)\) as income moves from −1.5 to 1.5 (with x2 equal to "Label 1"). Then recover it with comparisons().
Fifth, refit the model with brm(family = cumulative("logit")). Recover the cutpoints, the coefficients, and the first difference. Compare with polr() and the truth.


# --- simulate a fake data set ---

# set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(1234)

# set sample size
n <- 10000  # needs to be large enough so that CI isn't super wide

# create explanatory variables
## numeric variable; six brackets, like income in the anes data
income <- sample(c(-2.5, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5), size = n, replace = TRUE)
## qualitative variable
x2 <- sample(c("Label 1", "Label 2"),
             size = n,
             replace = TRUE,
             prob = c(0.75, 0.25))  # about 75% will be "Label 1"

# create cutpoints and coefficients
alpha <- c(-1, 0.5, 2)  # J - 1 = 3 cutpoints, so J = 4 categories
b1 <- 0.4
b2 <- 1

# linear predictor; no intercept!
eta <- b1*income + b2*(x2 == "Label 2")

# cumulative probabilities Pr(y <= j), j = 1, 2, 3
cp1 <- plogis(alpha[1] - eta)
cp2 <- plogis(alpha[2] - eta)
cp3 <- plogis(alpha[3] - eta)

# category probabilities Pr(y = j), j = 1, 2, 3, 4; one row per observation
p <- cbind(cp1, cp2 - cp1, cp3 - cp2, 1 - cp3)

# simulate outcome for ordered logit model; one draw per observation
y <- numeric(n)
for (i in 1:n) {
  y[i] <- sample(1:4, size = 1, prob = p[i, ])
}

# combine into data frame; y must be an ordered factor for polr()
data <- data.frame(y = factor(y, ordered = TRUE), income, x2)

# truth: Pr(y >= 3) when income = 1.5 and x2 = "Label 1"
eta_c <- b1*1.5  # x2 = "Label 1", so the b2 term is zero
1 - plogis(alpha[2] - eta_c)

[1] 0.5249792


Hint 1
\(\Pr(y \geq 3)\) is the sum of the probabilities of categories 3 and 4.

Week 6 added up category probabilities with hypothesis: Red State, Blue State: Part 2(a), part 3.


Hint 2

family = cumulative("logit").
fixef() labels the cutpoints Intercept[1], Intercept[2], and Intercept[3].
The same predictions() and comparisons() calls work on the brm() fit.


Complete solutionopens Oct 30, 12pm
Complete solution
Part 1
The true value of \(\Pr(y \geq 3)\) is about 0.525. Notice that \(\Pr(y \geq 3) = 1 - \Pr(y \leq 2) = 1 - \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_2 - \eta)\), so we only need the second cutpoint.
Part 2

# fit ordered logit model
fit <- MASS::polr(y ~ income + x2, data = data, Hess = TRUE)

# estimates and 95% cis for the coefficients and the cutpoints
est <- c(coef(fit), fit$zeta)
se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))
cbind(truth = c(b1, b2, alpha),
      estimate = est,
      lower = est - 1.96*se,
      upper = est + 1.96*se)

          truth   estimate      lower      upper
income      0.4  0.4090809  0.3867683  0.4313935
x2Label 2   1.0  0.9227028  0.8392080  1.0061975
1|2        -1.0 -1.0002890 -1.0507747 -0.9498033
2|3         0.5  0.5110824  0.4638427  0.5583221
3|4         2.0  2.0179461  1.9557867  2.0801055


All five true values are inside their 95% confidence intervals. The true value of b2 (i.e., 1) is only barely inside its interval (about 0.84 to 1.01); across many simulated data sets, we’d expect the interval to miss the true value about 5% of the time.
Part 3

# recover Pr(y >= 3) when income = 1.5 and x2 = "Label 1"
predictions(fit,
            newdata = datagrid(income = 1.5, x2 = "Label 1"),
            hypothesis = "b3 + b4 = 0")


 Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %
    b3+b4=0    0.526    0.00709 74.2   <0.001 Inf 0.512   0.54

Type: probs


The estimate is about 0.526, and the 95% CI runs from about 0.512 to 0.540. The true value (about 0.525) is inside the interval, as it usually will be.
Part 4

# truth: fd in Pr(y >= 3) as income moves from -1.5 to 1.5; x2 = "Label 1"
pr_hi <- 1 - plogis(alpha[2] - b1*1.5)
pr_lo <- 1 - plogis(alpha[2] - b1*(-1.5))
pr_hi - pr_lo

[1] 0.2752393

# recover this fd
comparisons(fit,

title: Week 10 Exercises
section: Exercise 4 Red State, Blue State: Part 6
text:
Exercise 4 Red State, Blue State: Part 6

Part 4 fit a separate logit in each state.
Now fit one hierarchical model to all 50 states. Each state gets its own intercept, and the 50 intercepts come from a normal distribution.
This is the varying-intercept model behind Figure 3 of Gelman et al. (2007, p. 355) [pdf].
income varies across voters within a state. rs_state_median_income varies only across states: state median household income, rescaled to mean 0 and SD 0.5 across the 50 states.
Same CES data as Part 4. The code below adds rs_state_median_income.


# load data; 50 states
ces <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/red-state-part4.csv")

Rows: 48582 Columns: 5
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): state_name, state_abbr
dbl (3): state_median_income, income, vote_rep

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

# one row per state; rescale state income to mean 0 and sd 0.5 across the 50 states
states <- ces |>
  distinct(state_name, state_abbr, state_median_income) |>
  mutate(rs_state_median_income = (state_median_income - mean(state_median_income)) /
           (2 * sd(state_median_income)))

# add rescaled state income to the voters
ces <- ces |>
  left_join(select(states, state_name, rs_state_median_income), by = "state_name")


Use brm() to fit the logit vote_rep ~ income + rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name). Use family = bernoulli, backend = "cmdstanr", iter = 10000, and warmup = 2000. Check R-hat and the ESS.
Use predictions() to compute Pr(Trump), with a 90% CI, for a voter in the middle income category (income = 0) in each state. Plot these 50 estimates and their CIs against state_median_income, labeled with the state abbreviations.
Add a line for a typical state (i.e., a state whose intercept is exactly what state income predicts). Use predictions() with re_formula = NA over a range of state incomes.
Interpret the coefficients on income and rs_state_median_income. Where does each show up in your plot? What is the vertical distance between a state’s point and the line?
In Part 4, the effect of income differed across states (e.g., about 0.15 in Mississippi and about −0.08 in Oregon). Does the effect of income differ across states in this model? Why or why not?
Gelman et al. (2007) describe a paradox: richer voters lean Republican, but richer states lean Democratic. Does this model show the same paradox in 2024?

Hint 1

Each state needs its own rs_state_median_income in the grid.
grid <- mutate(states, income = 0) gives one row per state.
predictions(fit, newdata = grid, conf_level = 0.9).


Hint 2

For the line: a grid of state incomes from the poorest state to the richest, rescaled the same way as rs_state_median_income, with income = 0.
re_formula = NA sets every state’s deviation to zero.


Complete solutionopens Oct 30, 12pm
Complete solution
Part 1

fit_ces <- brm(vote_rep ~ income + rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name),
               data = ces,
               family = bernoulli,
               backend = "cmdstanr",
               iter = 10000,
               warmup = 2000,
               chains = 4,
               cores = 4,
               seed = 1234)


summary(fit_ces)

  Links: mu = logit 
Formula: vote_rep ~ income + rs_state_median_income + (1 | state_name) 
   Data: ces (Number of observations: 48582)

         total post-warmup draws = 32000

Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).



R-hat 1.00 everywhere. Smallest bulk ESS above 2,000. Passes the notes’ rule of thumb.

Part 2

grid <- mutate(states, income = 0)

# pr(trump) with a 90% ci in each state
p_ces <- predictions(fit_ces, newdata = grid, conf_level = 0.9) |>
  as_tibble()


Plot under Part 3, with the line.

Part 3

# state incomes from the poorest state to the richest, rescaled like rs_state_median_income
line_grid <- tibble(state_median_income = seq(min(states$state_median_income),
                                              max(states$state_median_income),
                                              length.out = 50)) |>
  mutate(rs_state_median_income = (state_median_income - mean(states$state_median_income)) /
           (2 * sd(states$state_median_income)),
         income = 0)

# a typical state: every state's deviation set to zero
line_ces <- predictions(fit_ces, newdata = line_grid, re_formula = NA, conf_level = 0.9) |>
  as_tibble()


ggplot(p_ces, aes(x = state_median_income, y = estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = line_ces, aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = line_ces) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_text(aes(label = state_abbr), size = 3) +
  labs(x = "State median household income ($1,000s)",
       y = "Pr(Trump) for a voter with income = 0\n(90% CI)")








Part 4

# the two coefficients, with 90% intervals
posterior_summary(fit_ces,
                  variable = c("b_income", "b_rs_state_median_income"),
                  probs = c(0.05, 0.95)) |>
  round(3)

                         Estimate Est.Error     Q5    Q95
b_income                    0.011     0.008 -0.003  0.025
b_rs_state_median_income   -0.446     0.079 -0.575 -0.316

# one unit of rs_state_median_income is 2 sds of state median income ($1,000s)
2 * sd(states$state_median_income)

[1] 24.76068

# the line at the poorest and richest states
line_ces |>
  slice(1, n()) |>
  select(state_median_income, estimate)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  state_median_income estimate
                <dbl>    <dbl>
1                59.1    0.534
2               105.     0.335

# each state's distance from the line: its estimate minus a typical state's at the same state income
typical_ces <- predictions(fit_ces, newdata = grid, re_formula = NA) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(state_abbr, line = estimate)
distance_ces <- p_ces |>
  select(state_abbr, estimate) |>
  left_join(typical_ces, by = "state_abbr") |>
  mutate(distance = estimate - line) |>
  arrange(desc(distance))
head(distance_ces, 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  state_abbr estimate  line distance
  <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
1 ID            0.602 0.435   0.167 
2 WY            0.612 0.460   0.152 
3 UT            0.454 0.368   0.0861

tail(distance_ces, 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  state_abbr estimate  line distance
  <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
1 VT            0.347 0.428  -0.0810
2 MI            0.387 0.474  -0.0875
3 NM            0.400 0.495  -0.0948



income: 0.011 (90% interval from −0.003 to 0.025). Voters in the same state. By the divide-by-4 rule, at most about 0.003 per income category. Not in the plot (every point holds income at 0).
rs_state_median_income: −0.446 (from −0.575 to −0.316). States. The slope of the line. One unit is two SDs of state median income (about $24,800). The line falls from 0.534 (Mississippi, $59,100) to 0.335 (Massachusetts, $104,800).
Distance from the line: the state’s deviation from the varying-intercept model (on the probability scale), i.e., what state income doesn’t explain. Furthest above: Idaho (0.17), Wyoming (0.15), Utah (0.09). Furthest below: New Mexico (−0.09), Michigan (−0.09), Vermont (−0.08).

Part 5

# change in pr(trump) as income moves from -1 to 1 in each state
comparisons(fit_ces,
            variables = list(income = c(-1, 1)),
            newdata = grid,
            conf_level = 0.9) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarize(smallest = min(estimate), largest = max(estimate))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  smallest largest
     <dbl>   <dbl>
1  0.00484 0.00566



No. About 0.005 in every state (0.0048 to 0.0057).
Every state has the same coefficient on income. Only the intercepts vary.
The small differences come from the different baseline probabilities.
To let the effect differ across states: a varying slope, (1 + income | state_name).

Part 6

No. The paradox needs both halves.
Between states: still there. Richer states lean Democratic (−0.446).
Within states: gone. Richer voters are no more likely to vote for Trump (0.011; the 90% interval includes zero).
But Part 4 found larger effects in poorer states. A varying slope can check whether the average of about zero hides positive slopes in poor states.

text:
Exercise 5 Red State, Blue State: Part 7

Part 5 fit the separate logits to the ANES: wide CIs, extreme estimates from tiny states, and no estimates at all for Wyoming (1 respondent) or Vermont (2).
Now fit the hierarchical model from Exercise 4 to the ANES.


# load data; add rescaled state income from part 6
anes <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/red-state-part5.csv") |>
  left_join(select(states, state_name, rs_state_median_income), by = "state_name")

title: Week 10 Exercises
section: Exercise 6 Ordered or Not? Gelpi and Paolino
text:
Exercise 6 Ordered or Not? Gelpi and Paolino

March 2008 survey experiment on the war in Iraq (Gelpi; N = 1,000).
Each respondent read a short news story: successful military events in Iraq, unsuccessful events, or neither. Separately, a confident statement from President Bush (“no doubt … we will succeed”), a cautious statement, or neither.
Then: what do you think of a timetable for withdrawing all American troops from Iraq?
Paolino (2017): the answers are ordered. Ordered logit; the effects of the stories change linearly with approval of Bush.
Gelpi (2017): unordered. Multinomial logit, separately for each level of Bush approval.

Paolino, Philip. 2017. “Surprising Events and Surprising Opinions: The Importance of Attitude Strength and Source Credibility.” Journal of Conflict Resolution 61(8): 1795–1815.
Gelpi, Christopher. 2017. “The Surprising Robustness of Surprising Events.” Journal of Conflict Resolution 61(8): 1816–1834.

# load data
gelpi <- read_csv("https://pos5747.github.io/files/gelpi-iraq.csv")


timetable: “What do you think about the policy of setting a timetable with a specific date for withdrawing all American troops from Iraq?” Strongly approve, somewhat approve, somewhat disapprove, or strongly disapprove.
bush_approval: approval of President Bush, from 0 (strongly disapprove) to 3 (strongly approve).
pos_events, neg_events: 1 if the story reported successful (or unsuccessful) military events. No one read both.
pos_bush, neg_bush: 1 if the story included the confident (or cautious) statement from Bush. No one read both.

The code below orders the answers from most anti-war (“strongly approve” of a timetable) to most pro-war (“strongly disapprove”), and makes an unordered copy with “somewhat approve” as the baseline (as in Gelpi 2017).

gelpi_tt <- gelpi |>
  mutate(timetable = factor(timetable, levels = c("Strongly approve",
                                                  "Somewhat approve",
                                                  "Somewhat disapprove",
                                                  "Strongly disapprove")),
         timetable_nominal = relevel(factor(timetable, ordered = FALSE),
                                     ref = "Somewhat approve")) |>
  drop_na(timetable, bush_approval)


Fit Paolino’s ordered logit with MASS::polr(): timetable ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + neg_bush) * bush_approval. (A simplified version of the model in Paolino’s appendix Table A26, without the party dummies.)
Fit Gelpi’s multinomial logit with nnet::multinom(): timetable_nominal ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + neg_bush) * factor(bush_approval). (The same as Gelpi’s four separate models, one for each level of Bush approval.) How many parameters does each model have?
For each model, use comparisons() to compute the effect of positive events (pos_events from 0 to 1) on the probability of each of the four answers, at each level of Bush approval. Set the other three treatments to 0. Plot the effects with their 95% CIs, with one panel for each level of Bush approval and both models in each panel.
Among strong Bush disapprovers (bush_approval = 0), how do positive events change the four probabilities in the multinomial logit? Could the ordered logit produce this pattern? How strong is the evidence for it?
Compare the two models with AIC and BIC. Which does each prefer?
Which model would you report? Why?

Hint 1

datagrid(model = fit, pos_events = 0, neg_events = 0, pos_bush = 0, neg_bush = 0, bush_approval = 0:3) as newdata.
For the multinomial logit, add type = "probs".
The group column holds the answer.


Hint 2
For part 4: under the ordered logit, \(\Pr(Y_i = 1) = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_1 - \eta_i)\) and \(\Pr(Y_i = 4) = 1 - \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_3 - \eta_i)\). What happens to each as \(\eta_i\) increases? As \(\eta_i\) decreases?

Complete solutionopens Oct 30, 12pm
Complete solution
Part 1

# paolino: ordered logit, each treatment interacted with bush approval
fit_ordered <- MASS::polr(timetable ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + neg_bush) * bush_approval,
                          data = gelpi_tt, Hess = TRUE)
summary(fit_ordered)

Call:
MASS::polr(formula = timetable ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + 
    neg_bush) * bush_approval, data = gelpi_tt, Hess = TRUE)

Coefficients:

pos_events                0.08298     0.1985  0.41796
neg_events               -0.16464     0.1947 -0.84542
pos_bush                 -0.01505     0.1968 -0.07645
neg_bush                  0.11826     0.1969  0.60055
bush_approval             1.09310     0.1270  8.60708
pos_events:bush_approval  0.17327     0.1440  1.20293
neg_events:bush_approval  0.13646     0.1419  0.96196
pos_bush:bush_approval    0.01084     0.1509  0.07183
neg_bush:bush_approval   -0.32012     0.1389 -2.30452

Intercepts:
                                        Value   Std. Error t value
Strongly approve|Somewhat approve       -0.5815  0.1794    -3.2407
Somewhat approve|Somewhat disapprove     0.9721  0.1802     5.3949
Somewhat disapprove|Strongly disapprove  2.0710  0.1915    10.8144

Residual Deviance: 2360.836 
AIC: 2384.836 


Part 2

# gelpi: multinomial logit, a separate set of effects for each level of bush approval
fit_multinomial <- nnet::multinom(timetable_nominal ~ (pos_events + neg_events + pos_bush + neg_bush) * factor(bush_approval),
                                  data = gelpi_tt, trace = FALSE)

# number of parameters
attr(logLik(fit_ordered), "df")

[1] 12

attr(logLik(fit_multinomial), "df")

[1] 60



Ordered logit: 12 (nine coefficients and three cutpoints).
Multinomial logit: 60 (3 equations × 5 coefficients × 4 levels of Bush approval).

Part 3

# no other story, each level of bush approval
grid_ordered <- datagrid(model = fit_ordered, pos_events = 0, neg_events = 0,
                         pos_bush = 0, neg_bush = 0, bush_approval = 0:3)
grid_multinomial <- datagrid(model = fit_multinomial, pos_events = 0, neg_events = 0,
                             pos_bush = 0, neg_bush = 0, bush_approval = 0:3)

# effect of positive events on each probability
# (the multinomial logit returns bush_approval as a factor, so make both numeric)
c_ordered <- comparisons(fit_ordered, variables = "pos_events", newdata = grid_ordered) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(bush_approval = as.numeric(as.character(bush_approval)))
c_multinomial <- comparisons(fit_multinomial, variables = "pos_events",
                             newdata = grid_multinomial, type = "probs") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(bush_approval = as.numeric(as.character(bush_approval)))

# both models
c_both <- bind_rows(list(`Ordered logit` = c_ordered,
                         `Multinomial logit` = c_multinomial), .id = "model")


ggplot(c_both, aes(x = estimate, xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high, y = group,
                   color = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), size = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(vars(bush_approval), nrow = 1, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(levels(gelpi_tt$timetable))) +  # scale order, top to bottom
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.2, 0, 0.2)) +
  labs(x = "Effect of positive events on the probability (95% CI)",
       y = NULL,
       color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Part 4

# the strong disapprovers
c_both |>
  filter(bush_approval == 0) |>
  select(model, group, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

# A tibble: 8 × 5
  model             group               estimate conf.low conf.high
  <chr>             <fct>                  <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Ordered logit     Strongly approve    -0.0189  -0.107     0.0695 
2 Ordered logit     Somewhat approve     0.00202 -0.00799   0.0120 
3 Ordered logit     Somewhat disapprove  0.00831 -0.0307    0.0473 
4 Ordered logit     Strongly disapprove  0.00852 -0.0316    0.0486 
5 Multinomial logit Somewhat approve    -0.117   -0.228    -0.00509
6 Multinomial logit Strongly approve     0.0604  -0.0493    0.170  
7 Multinomial logit Somewhat disapprove -0.0111  -0.0983    0.0760 
8 Multinomial logit Strongly disapprove  0.0675   0.00117   0.134  



Multinomial logit: Pr(somewhat approve) falls by 0.12 (95% CI from −0.23 to −0.005). Pr(strongly disapprove) rises by 0.07 (from 0.001 to 0.13). Pr(strongly approve) rises by 0.06 (from −0.05 to 0.17). Out of the middle, toward both ends.
The ordered logit can’t do this.

As \(\eta_i\) increases, \(\alpha_1 - \eta_i\) and \(\alpha_3 - \eta_i\) both decrease. \(\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\) is increasing, so \(\Pr(Y_i = 1)\) falls and \(\Pr(Y_i = 4)\) rises.
As \(\eta_i\) decreases, both reverse.
A treatment shifts \(\eta_i\) by the same amount for everyone at a level of Bush approval, so its effects on the two end categories have opposite signs (or are both zero).
Ordered logit here: −0.02 on “strongly approve” and 0.01 on “strongly disapprove.”

Weak evidence. The pattern depends on the rise in “strongly approve,” and that interval includes zero.

Part 5

tibble(model = c("Ordered logit", "Multinomial logit"),
       parameters = c(attr(logLik(fit_ordered), "df"), attr(logLik(fit_multinomial), "df")),
       log_lik = c(logLik(fit_ordered), logLik(fit_multinomial)),
       aic = c(AIC(fit_ordered), AIC(fit_multinomial)),
       bic = c(BIC(fit_ordered), BIC(fit_multinomial)))

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  model             parameters log_lik   aic   bic
  <chr>                  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Ordered logit             12  -1180. 2385. 2444.
2 Multinomial logit         60  -1146. 2413. 2707.



Multinomial logit: 34 more in log-likelihood for 48 more parameters.
AIC (2,385 vs. 2,413) and BIC (2,444 vs. 2,707) both prefer the ordered logit.

Part 6

No single right answer. Ours: the ordered logit, with the multinomial logit as a check.
AIC and BIC prefer it.
The one pattern it can’t produce rests on an interval that includes zero.
118 to 450 respondents per level of Bush approval: the multinomial logit’s 60 parameters are imprecise. Notice its wider intervals in the plot.

title: Suggestions for the Exercises
text:
Answer the questions in a Quarto document that compiles to PDF. Make sure that all your code is neat and readable, equations are typeset nicely with LaTeX, and figures render nicely. The Quarto documentation is excellent.

For mathematical problems, work out the answers with paper-and-pencil first, then move the answers to a Quarto document (while simultaneously reviewing and polishing).
For coding problems, write and debug the code in a standalone .R script first, then move the code to a Quarto code chunk.

At the beginning of the semester, start a new R project called exr/. Each week, create a new .qmd document named wk01-exr.qmd, wk02-exr.qmd, …, in exr/. (You can adjust these names if you like.) Throughout the semester you’ll have several PDFs that you can revise and review as you prepare for the exams.
Make sure to render often as you work in a .qmd file (e.g., every time you add a new part).
Use the {tinytable} package to automate table creation.
The default output of tt(), modelsummary(), ggplot(), etc. is almost always “good enough” for our purposes. Don’t spend lots of time polishing your tables, plots, and output. Use that time and energy to focus on understanding the ideas, math, and code.
An exception to the rule above is carefully controlling the output of code chunks. In most cases, you want messages: false and warnings: false. You don’t want a lot of junk in your rendered documents, but it’s fine if your column and axis labels have the raw variable names.
